events.title: Gore carries Michigan
events.text: Al Gore won Michigan by about five points, part of a Democratic run in presidential races from 1992 to 2012.

events.title: Granholm elected
events.text: Jennifer Granholm, the attorney general, won the open governor's seat for the Democrats after twelve years of John Engler.

events.title: Kerry by 3.4
events.text: John Kerry carried Michigan by 3.4 points.

events.title: Granholm re-elected
events.text: Granholm beat Dick DeVos of Ada by fourteen points.

events.title: Obama by 16
events.text: Barack Obama carried Michigan by 16.5 points.

events.title: GM and Chrysler
events.text: Chrysler in April and General Motors in June went through federally backed bankruptcies.

events.title: Snyder elected
events.text: Rick Snyder, a Republican businessman from Ann Arbor, won the open seat with 58 percent.

events.title: Right-to-work law
events.text: In December Michigan became a right-to-work state, in the home of the United Auto Workers.

events.title: Detroit bankruptcy
events.text: On 18 July Detroit filed the largest municipal bankruptcy in U.S. history.

events.title: Flint's water
events.text: In April Flint switched its water supply to the Flint River, starting the Flint water crisis.

events.title: Duggan becomes mayor
events.text: Mike Duggan became mayor of Detroit in January; he served until the end of 2025.

events.title: Snyder re-elected
events.text: Snyder beat Mark Schauer by four points.

events.title: 10,704 votes
events.text: Donald Trump carried Michigan by 10,704 votes, the first Republican presidential win there since 1988.

events.title: Voting rights amendment
events.text: Voters approved Proposal 3, adding no-excuse absentee voting and same-day registration to the constitution, with 66.9 percent.

events.title: Whitmer elected
events.text: Gretchen Whitmer beat Bill Schuette by 9.6 points for the open governor's seat.

events.title: Benson elected
events.text: Jocelyn Benson, a former law-school dean, was elected Secretary of State, Michigan's chief election officer.

events.title: James's first race
events.text: John James, a Detroit businessman and Army veteran, lost a U.S. Senate race to Debbie Stabenow, 45.8 to 52.3 percent.

events.title: Applications by mail
events.text: Benson mailed absentee-ballot applications to all voters; the courts upheld her authority.

events.title: Biden by 2.8
events.text: Joe Biden carried Michigan by 2.8 points; 3.3 million of 5.5 million voters voted absentee.

events.title: Peters edges James
events.text: Senator Gary Peters beat John James by 1.7 points.

events.title: Plot against Whitmer
events.text: In October the FBI charged men who had plotted to kidnap Governor Whitmer.

events.title: Abortion rights amendment
events.text: Voters approved Proposal 3, writing abortion rights into the state constitution.

events.title: Early voting
events.text: Voters approved Proposal 2, guaranteeing at least nine days of early in-person voting.

events.title: Whitmer re-elected
events.text: Whitmer beat Tudor Dixon by 10.5 points; Democrats also won both chambers of the Legislature.

events.title: James wins a House seat
events.text: James won the new 10th district in Macomb and Oakland counties by half a point.

events.title: Right-to-work repealed
events.text: Michigan became the first state in decades to repeal a right-to-work law.

events.title: UAW strike
events.text: The United Auto Workers struck all three Detroit automakers at once for the first time.

events.title: Uncommitted
events.text: In the February primary, about 101,000 Democratic voters chose 'uncommitted', a protest led from Dearborn over the war in Gaza.

events.title: Trump by 1.4
events.text: Donald Trump carried Michigan by 1.4 points; he carried Macomb County by 13.7.

events.title: Slotkin wins
events.text: On the same ballot, Democrat Elissa Slotkin won the open Senate seat by 0.3 points: many voters split their tickets.

events.title: Duggan goes independent
events.text: On 4 December Mike Duggan left the Democratic Party to run for governor as an independent.

events.title: Benson enters
events.text: On 22 January Jocelyn Benson announced her campaign for governor.

events.title: James enters
events.text: On 7 April John James announced his campaign for governor.

events.title: Gilchrist switches race
events.text: On 12 January Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist left the governor's race to run for Secretary of State.

events.title: Duggan ends bid
events.text: On 21 May Duggan ended his independent campaign, saying he was running 'to change politics, not to be a spoiler'.

events.title: Trump endorses James
events.text: On 22 June President Trump endorsed James.

events.title: Primary day
events.text: On 4 August Benson won the Democratic primary with 83 percent and James the Republican primary with 50.

events.title: Running mates
events.text: James chose state Rep. Jay DeBoyer (13 Aug); Benson chose Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks, of Grand Rapids (19 Aug).

events.title: Libertarians disavow nominee
events.text: On 27 September the Libertarian Party disavowed its nominee, Anthony Hudson, who remains on the ballot.

events.title: First debate
events.text: On 6 October Benson and James debated in Grand Rapids.

events.title: Second debate
events.text: On 15 October Benson and James debated again, at WDIV's studios in Detroit.

events.title: Early voting
events.text: At least nine days of early in-person voting run from 24 October to 1 November.

events.title: Election Day
events.text: On 3 November Michigan chooses between five tickets for governor and lieutenant governor.

eras: Granholm's Michigan and the auto crisis
The Whitmer years and an open seat
chartNote: Each state is coloured by the margin of the most recent presidential popular vote (Democratic minus Republican share of all votes; FEC certified results). It is a simplification: Michigan elects its governor in its own race, in the midterm years, and many Michiganders split their tickets (in 2024 the state voted Republican for president and Democratic for the Senate), so the presidential colour is a backdrop, not a forecast; the governor's results are given in Michigan's notes. Shares are of land area, not of people or votes. Boundaries are today's states (Natural Earth); the map is framed on Michigan and the Great Lakes, so outer states are cut at the edge.
